title: How to Wholesale Commercial Property: A Step-by-Step Guide for Real Estate Investors
excerpt: Commercial wholesaling offers bigger assignment fees and less competition than residential deals — but the process works differently. This guide walks you through exactly how to wholesale commercial property, from finding deals to closing your first assignment.
author: AIWholesail Team
metaDescription: Learn how to wholesale commercial property step by step. Find deals, analyze numbers, and close assignments with bigger profits than residential wholesaling.

sections.content: Most people think of wholesaling as a residential game — finding distressed single-family homes and flipping contracts to cash buyers. But there is a bigger, less crowded arena that experienced investors are quietly profiting from: commercial property wholesaling. Assignment fees on commercial deals can range from $20,000 to well over $100,000, and the buyers on the other end are sophisticated enough to close fast. If you have ever wondered how to wholesale commercial property, this guide breaks down every step in plain language.
What Is Commercial Property Wholesaling?

Commercial wholesaling follows the same core principle as residential wholesaling: you get a property under contract at a price below market value, then assign that contract to an end buyer for a fee. The difference is the asset type. Commercial properties include office buildings, retail strip centers, industrial warehouses, self-storage facilities, apartment complexes with five or more units, and mixed-use buildings. Because the dollar amounts are larger, the due diligence is more thorough and the buyer pool is smaller — but the paydays reflect that. If you are new to wholesaling in general, start with our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide before diving into the commercial side.
Step 1 — Learn the Commercial Metrics That Drive Value

Residential values are based on comparable sales. Commercial values are based on income. This is the most important mindset shift you need to make. The two numbers every commercial wholesaler must understand are Net Operating Income (NOI) and Cap Rate. NOI is the property's gross rental income minus operating expenses (not including debt service). Cap Rate is the NOI divided by the purchase price. A $500,000 building generating $40,000 in NOI has an 8% cap rate. If the local market trades at a 7% cap rate, that same NOI supports a value closer to $571,000 — meaning there is room to negotiate and still leave a buyer with a good deal.

Before making any offer, run the numbers with a dedicated tool. Use our free [Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) at AIWholesail to quickly check if a commercial deal has enough margin for an assignment fee after accounting for repairs, carrying costs, and buyer profit requirements.
Step 2 — Find Motivated Commercial Sellers

Motivated sellers exist in commercial real estate just like in residential. Common situations include aging landlords tired of managing tenants, owners facing loan maturity defaults, inherited commercial properties, businesses that closed and left the owner with a vacant building, and properties with deferred maintenance that scare off traditional buyers. These sellers want speed and certainty over top dollar.
Where to Find Off-Market Commercial Deals

items: County tax records — search for properties with delinquent taxes or out-of-state ownership
Direct mail campaigns targeting commercial property owners in specific zip codes
Commercial real estate brokers who specialize in distressed or value-add assets
Networking at local REIA meetings where commercial investors congregate
LoopNet and CoStar — filter for properties with long days on market (90+ days is a signal)
Driving for dollars in commercial corridors — look for vacant storefronts and neglected parking lots
Probate and bankruptcy court filings — these often surface motivated commercial sellers quickly

sections.content: Active commercial markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) have strong investor demand, meaning you will have a larger pool of end buyers ready to close once you lock in a good deal. Markets with population growth and job creation are ideal for your first commercial wholesale because buyers are actively competing for deals.
Step 3 — Analyze the Deal Before Making an Offer

Analyzing a commercial deal correctly is what separates professionals from beginners. You need to request the rent roll (a list of all current tenants, lease terms, and monthly rents), the last 12 to 24 months of operating statements, property tax bills, insurance costs, and any known capital expenditure needs. From there, calculate the actual NOI — not the pro forma numbers the seller gives you. Sellers routinely project optimistic occupancy rates. Use actual vacancy to build your conservative case. For a deeper look at deal analysis fundamentals, see our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals).
Quick Example: Analyzing a Small Retail Strip Center

Say you find a 4-unit retail strip center in a growing suburb. The owner says it grosses $8,000 per month ($96,000 per year). After reviewing actual leases, you find one unit is month-to-month and another is 60 days vacant. Realistic gross income is closer to $72,000. Operating expenses (taxes, insurance, management, maintenance) total $22,000 per year. That gives you a real NOI of $50,000. If the local market cap rate is 7.5%, the property is worth roughly $667,000. If the seller needs to move fast and will accept $540,000, you have found a potential deal. You could put it under contract at $540,000 and assign it to a buyer at $575,000 — a $35,000 assignment fee — while still delivering real value to your buyer.
Step 4 — Structure the Contract Correctly

Commercial purchase and sale agreements are more complex than residential contracts. They typically include longer inspection periods (30 to 60 days is common), environmental contingencies, financing contingencies, and specific representations from the seller about tenant leases. Make sure your contract explicitly allows assignment, or use a separate assignment agreement. Some wholesalers use an LLC to purchase and then sell the LLC membership interest rather than assigning the contract — this can be cleaner in commercial deals and avoids some transfer tax issues. Always work with a real estate attorney familiar with commercial transactions in your state.
In commercial real estate, the contract is your product. A well-structured purchase agreement with the right contingencies and a clear assignment clause is worth more than any marketing campaign.
Step 5 — Build Your Commercial Buyer List

Commercial buyers are not your typical fix-and-flip investors. They include private equity firms, family offices, 1031 exchange buyers, real estate syndicators, and local operators who own multiple commercial assets. The best way to find them is to attend commercial real estate networking events, join local and national commercial real estate associations, and connect with commercial brokers who can introduce you to active buyers. When you do have a deal, send a well-formatted one-page deal summary with the address (or just the market if you want to keep it off-market), property type, square footage, current NOI, asking price, and cap rate. Make it easy for busy buyers to say yes.

Build your buyer list before you have a deal, not after. Reach out to 20 to 30 commercial investors in your target market and simply ask what type of commercial assets they are buying and what returns they need. This research makes you sharper at underwriting and gives you a ready list when you lock up your first contract.
Common Mistakes to Avoid in Commercial Wholesaling

items: Relying on seller-provided pro forma numbers instead of verified actuals
Using a residential purchase contract for a commercial property — always use the right documents
Skipping environmental due diligence on industrial or gas station properties
Not having an assignability clause in your purchase agreement
Underestimating the inspection period needed — 30 days minimum for commercial
Targeting asset types with thin buyer pools (very niche properties in small markets)
Quoting an assignment fee before you fully understand what your end buyer will pay

sections.content: Is Commercial Wholesaling Right for You?

Commercial wholesaling is not a starting point for most investors — it rewards those who have built some foundational knowledge of real estate deal flow and analysis. The deals take longer to close, require more due diligence, and demand a higher level of professionalism from your buyers, attorneys, and brokers. But the margins are real, the competition is lower than in residential wholesaling, and one successful commercial assignment can equal 10 residential deals. If you are ready to move up in scale, commercial wholesaling is one of the highest-leverage ways to do it.
